story: Flock plate readers reach Anchorage Lowe's stores while the Assembly weighs three versions of its surveillance ordinance, AO 2026-108, before an October 20th meeting

claims.claim: Anchorage ordinance AO 2026-108, as introduced, repeals and replaces Anchorage Municipal Code chapter 3.102 and amends section 7.15.040.
claims.verbatim: Ordinance No. AO 2026-108, an ordinance of the Anchorage Municipal Assembly repealing and replacing Anchorage Municipal Code Chapter 3.102 and amending AMC Section 7.15.040
claims.source_outlet: Municipality of Anchorage, Municipal Clerk's Office public notice
claims.notes: Read via r.jina.ai. The verbatim joins line-broken fragments of the notice title. Notice runs August 20th to September 2nd, signed by Municipal Clerk Jamie Heinz. The ordinance PDF title (https://www.muni.org/Departments/Assembly/SiteAssets/Pages/focus-on-public-safety/AO%202026-108_1_Surveillance_Technology_Final.pdf) reads 'AN ORDINANCE OF THE ANCHORAGE MUNICIPAL ASSEMBLY REPEALING AND REPLACING ANCHORAGE MUNICIPAL CODE CHAPTER 3.102'. The sponsors' memo AM 554-2026 says the existing facial recognition, drone and body camera language is preserved and relocated. BACKGROUND date. This describes the August 18th original only; the September 15th versions (C30, C37) amend chapter 3.102 instead.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 was submitted by Assembly Members Keith McCormick and Sydney Scout and Vice Chair Daniel Volland, for reading on August 18th.
claims.verbatim: Submitted by: Assembly Member McCormick Assembly Vice Chair Volland Assembly Member Scout Prepared by: Assembly Legal Services For reading: August 18, 2026
claims.notes: Read via r.jina.ai (23 pages). Header lines joined; extraction places a stray '1' before 'Assembly Member Scout'. The sponsors' memo AM 554-2026 (meeting date August 18th) is signed by the same three members. Background.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 requires captured license plate data to be permanently deleted no later than fourteen days after capture.
claims.verbatim: Captured plate data shall be permanently deleted no later than fourteen days after capture, unless otherwise specified in this section.
claims.notes: Section 3.102.030(C)(1). STATUS: this number is in the August 18th original only; neither (S) nor (S-1) contains a day count (C29, C73, C74). Never write that a 14-day limit is up for a vote October 20th. Write 'the original version would have required'. APD's page already says scanned plate data is deleted after 14 days (C38). Amended October 10th: source is the ordinance text PDF AO 2026-108_1.

claims.claim: The sponsors' memo says license plate reader data, camera footage and Real Time Crime Center recordings would have to be deleted within fourteen days unless designated as evidence or preserved under a warrant, litigation hold or public records request.
claims.verbatim: ALPR data, camera footage, and real-time crime center recordings must be deleted within fourteen days unless individually designated as evidence or preserved under a warrant, litigation hold, or public records request
claims.notes: This is the sponsors' memo summarizing the original ordinance, NOT the ordinance text; the scout brief mislabeled this PDF as the ordinance. Read via r.jina.ai. The page prints 'real ‑time' with a non-breaking hyphen, normalized here; the verbatim joins two returned fragments. The memo also says 'Bulk or automatic retention is prohibited'.

claims.claim: Under the original AO 2026-108, a search of plate data more than fourteen days old would also require a warrant issued on probable cause.
claims.verbatim: A query of captured plate data more than fourteen days old shall additionally require a warrant issued upon probable cause
claims.notes: Section 3.102.100(C)(2). The exception is 'where necessary to address an imminent threat to human life', and in that case a written report goes to the chief of police within twenty-four hours and is disclosed in the Annual Surveillance Report. Section 3.102.100(C)(1) requires every query to record the user, date and time, a valid case number and a specific written justification. Not in the (S) or (S-1) versions. Same status caution as C03.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 limits real-time plate reader alerts to a hot list of five categories, stolen vehicles or plates, AMBER or Silver Alert subjects, people with outstanding felony warrants, and vehicles in active felony or missing person investigations.
claims.verbatim: An ALPR system may compare captured plate data in real time against a hot list limited to vehicles
claims.notes: Section 3.102.060(B), five numbered items. 1 'Reported stolen, or that bear license plates reported stolen'. 2 'The subject of an active AMBER Alert, Silver Alert, or comparable emergency alert concerning a missing or endangered person'. 3 'Registered to a person for whom an outstanding felony warrant has been issued'. 4 'Specifically identified in an active, documented investigation of a felony offense'. 5 'Specifically identified in an active, documented investigation of a missing or endangered person.' 'Five' is our count of the numbered list.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 bars using plate readers to investigate or enforce any suspected misdemeanor, minor offense, infraction or civil violation.
claims.verbatim: An ALPR system shall not be used for investigation or enforcement of any suspected misdemeanor or minor offense, infraction, or civil violation.
claims.notes: Section 3.102.060(B). The sponsors' memo AM 554-2026 agrees: 'They may not be used for misdemeanors'.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 would end the city's plate reader authorization on January 1st, 2031, unless the Assembly renews it by ordinance.
claims.verbatim: repealed by operation of law effective January 1, 2031
claims.notes: Section 3.102.060(C). The sponsors' memo says 'ending the authorization in 2031 unless affirmatively renewed.' (S) and (S-1) contain no '2031' or 'sunset' (C73, C74). Amended October 10th: source is the ordinance text PDF AO 2026-108_1.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 requires Assembly approval before any city agency acquires surveillance technology, including through a free trial, demonstration or beta test.
claims.verbatim: This prohibition shall apply to any free trial, demonstration, beta test, or other temporary acquisition
claims.notes: Section 3.102.020(C)(1). The public notice title includes 'to require assembly approval for the acquisition of surveillance technology'. The sponsors' memo says the existing facial recognition approval procedure in AMC 3.102.020F is extended 'to the acquisition of any surveillance technology', and that 'the Assembly, not vendors, controls surveillance capability' (dash spacing normalized).

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 lets the Assembly grant a temporary approval of new surveillance technology for no longer than 90 days, by resolution after a public hearing.
claims.verbatim: for a period of no longer than 90 days, if it finds that the exception is consistent with the stated goals of preventing discrimination and promoting privacy
claims.notes: Section 3.102.020(C)(1)(b). The memo calls it 'a 90 day trial period'. (S) and (S-1) instead exempt tests and pilots with no stated time limit (C34). Amended October 10th: source is the ordinance text PDF AO 2026-108_1.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 requires an annual compliance audit by the municipal ombudsman, or by internal audit at the Assembly's direction.
claims.verbatim: The municipal ombudsman, or internal audit at the direction of the Assembly, shall conduct an annual audit
claims.notes: Section 3.102.050(A). The memo says the audit reviews 'logs, retention settings, access controls' and 'samples of live monitoring sessions.' The (S) and (S-1) versions instead require each policy to provide 'periodic review of the audit trail' with no set frequency.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 requires the mayor or a designee to submit an Annual Surveillance Report no later than June 1st each year.
claims.verbatim: No later than June 1 of each year, the mayor or a designee shall submit to
claims.notes: Section 3.102.040, continuing 'the Annual Surveillance Report with all the information required by this section'. The mayor's (S) version keeps the same June 1 deadline ('No later than June 1 of each year', section 3.102.040A).

claims.claim: Under the original AO 2026-108, the chief of police must certify in each annual report that automated deletion is configured and working.
claims.verbatim: The chief of police shall certify in the Annual Surveillance Report that automated deletion is configured and functioning
claims.notes: Section 3.102.030(C)(5). The memo agrees: 'the chief of police must annually certify that automated deletion is functioning.'

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 bars city agencies from joining, contributing data to or querying any external surveillance data network.
claims.verbatim: No municipal agency shall join, subscribe to, participate in, contribute surveillance data to, query, receive surveillance data from, or enable interoperability with any external surveillance data network.
claims.notes: Section 3.102.020(A)(2). The ordinance doesn't name Flock. In S-1 the phrase appears only as struck title text (C36). Amended October 10th: source is the ordinance text PDF AO 2026-108_1.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 defines surveillance technology as any software, device or system used to collect, retain, analyze, process or share information that can be associated with any individual, vehicle or group.
claims.verbatim: Surveillance technology means any software, electronic device, or system used, designed, or primarily intended to collect, retain, analyze, process, or share audio, electronic, visual, location, thermal, olfactory, biometric, or similar information
claims.notes: Section 3.102.010, continuing 'specifically associated with, or capable of being associated with, any individual, vehicle, or group.' Amended October 10th: source is the ordinance text PDF AO 2026-108_1.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 defines a license plate reader system to include fixed, mobile, semi-stationary, aerial and handheld systems, and any system that searches vehicles by traits other than the plate number.
claims.verbatim: whether fixed, mobile, semi-stationary, aerial, or handheld
claims.notes: Section 3.102.010. Full definition opens 'Automated license plate reader (ALPR) system means any system, device, software, algorithm, or combination thereof' and ends 'The term includes any system that identifies, classifies, or enables the search of vehicles by characteristics other than license plate number.'

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 bars city agencies from using predictive analytics to forecast where crime will happen.
claims.verbatim: No municipal agency shall use predictive analytics to forecast the location of future criminal activity
claims.notes: Section 3.102.100(D). One scan of the original found no 'artificial intelligence' or 'machine learning'; the AI wording enters with (S) (C30) and S-1 (C75). Amended October 10th: source is the ordinance text PDF AO 2026-108_1.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 makes it unlawful for the city or its staff to use facial recognition with any real-time surveillance or surveillance technology.
claims.verbatim: The use of facial recognition technology in conjunction with, or as a component of, any real-time surveillance or surveillance technology by the municipality or any municipal staff shall be unlawful.
claims.notes: Section 3.102.080(A). The sponsors' memo says this language is relocated from existing code. The 2023 ban is C39. Amended October 10th: source is the ordinance text PDF AO 2026-108_1.

claims.claim: Under the original AO 2026-108, registering a private camera with the city doesn't let the city access it, and an integrated live feed needs the owner's written, informed and revocable consent.
claims.verbatim: Registration of a camera under this subsection does not authorize the municipality to access that camera.
claims.notes: Section 3.102.100(C)(2). (C)(3) reads 'An integrated camera feed shall be established only upon the written, informed, and revocable' consent; (C)(14) bars remote control 'unless the owner has separately and expressly consented in writing'; (C)(15) 'Audio from an integrated camera feed shall be disabled by default'. SCOPE. The core rules bind municipal agencies ('No municipal agency shall possess or use surveillance technology', 3.102.020(A)). Private cameras appear only where they connect to the city. Nothing read regulates a private business's own plate readers, such as the Lowe's cameras.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 would cut off live camera access automatically after sixty minutes, with each renewal limited to thirty minutes.
claims.verbatim: The system shall automatically terminate live access after sixty minutes
claims.notes: Section 3.102.100(C)(11), which also reads 'Each renewal shall be limited to thirty minutes.' (C)(9) bars 'continuous, random, generalized, or location-based observation', and (C)(13) bars using feeds to 'follow, reidentify, or reconstruct the movements' of people.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 gives people harmed by a violation a right to sue for at least $1,000 per violation or $10,000, whichever is greater.
claims.verbatim: shall be entitled to recover actual damages of not less than the greater of: $1,000.00 for each violation of this chapter; or $10,000.00.
claims.notes: Section 3.102.050(C)(2)(a) and (b), joined. Evidence gathered in violation can't be offered in municipal proceedings except where exculpatory (B)(3). The (S) and (S-1) versions reference a private cause of action but no damages figure appeared in the extraction.

claims.claim: The original AO 2026-108 would take effect ninety days after passage, except its Assembly approval requirement, which would apply immediately.
claims.verbatim: This ordinance shall be effective ninety days after passage and approval by the Assembly, except the requirements of AMC subsection 3.102.020C. shall be effective immediately
claims.notes: Section 5. The (S) and (S-1) versions say 'effective 30 days after passage and approval by the Assembly' (Section 9).

claims.claim: The city's public notice set a public hearing on AO 2026-108 for the Assembly's September 1st regular meeting.
claims.verbatim: will hold a public hearing on the following legislation at its regular meeting of September 1, 2026.
claims.source_outlet: Municipality of Anchorage, Municipal Clerk's Office public notice
claims.notes: Read via r.jina.ai. Hearing at 6 p.m. in the Assembly Chambers, Z.J. Loussac Library. Background. The Assembly's focus-on-public-safety page says the hearing was continued September 1st and 'continued and closed' September 15th.

claims.claim: The Anchorage Assembly's own ordinance page says it voted to postpone further action on AO 2026-108 to October 20th.
claims.verbatim: The Anchorage Assembly voted to postpone further action on AO 2026-108 to October 20.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Assembly, Focus on Public Safety page
claims.notes: Read via r.jina.ai October 10th. The page is undated, so date_of_source is null. The same page also lists a second work session on AO 2026-108 on October 14th; its listed time looked garbled in extraction, so don't print a time. Corroborated by the Anchorage Daily News, September 16th (C25). date_of_source is the fetch date, the page is undated.

claims.claim: The Assembly voted unanimously in mid September to postpone further discussion of surveillance regulations to its October 20th regular meeting, according to the Anchorage Daily News.
claims.verbatim: postpone further discussions on surveillance regulations until its regular meeting Oct. 20
claims.notes: By Bella Biondini. The article says the Assembly 'voted unanimously'. Volland said the sponsors couldn't reach full agreement with the administration and that 'stronger language and stronger protections' were needed. Mayor LaFrance told the Assembly 'Given how quickly technology is changing, this conversation will need to continue.' Background.

claims.claim: Two surveillance proposals, one from Mayor Suzanne LaFrance's administration and one from a group of Assembly members, are expected to go before the Assembly for a vote on October 20th, according to the Anchorage Daily News.
claims.verbatim: Those measures are expected to go before the Assembly for a vote on Oct. 20.
claims.notes: By Zachariah Hughes; page shows Published October 7th, URL path 10/06. NEEDS SOFTENING. Keep 'expected to'. ADN does not name the versions by number. The Assembly page lists three texts: the original, the mayor's (S) and the sponsors' (S-1), which revises (S). No fetched source says which sponsors' text is the October 20th vehicle. Primary date corroboration in C24.

claims.claim: Mayor LaFrance's substitute, AO 2026-108(S), was submitted by the Assembly chair at the mayor's request, prepared by the Department of Law, for reading on September 15th.
claims.verbatim: Submitted by: Chair of the Assembly at the Request of the Mayor
claims.notes: Read via r.jina.ai (14 pages including the mayor's memo AM 603-2026, marked 'FROM: MAYOR', meeting date September 15th). Other lines 'Prepared by: Dept. of Law' and 'For reading: September 15, 2026'. Background.

claims.claim: The mayor's memo says the substitute amends chapter 3.102 rather than repealing and replacing it.
claims.verbatim: is drafted as amending existing Chapter 3.102 (using legislative formatting to reflect changes to existing municipal code), rather than repealing and replacing it.
claims.notes: The memo also says the substitute 'takes a more streamlined, focused approach to this subject than the original ordinance.' The S title opens 'AN ORDINANCE OF THE ANCHORAGE MUNICIPAL ASSEMBLY AMENDING ANCHORAGE MUNICIPAL CODE CHAPTER 3.102'.

claims.claim: The mayor's substitute requires the city's plate reader policy to limit storage of non-evidence data based on articulable operational needs, without setting a number of days.
claims.verbatim: contains a limitation, based on articulable operational needs, on the storage of surveillance data collected by ALPR that is not retained as evidence in a specific case or investigation;
claims.notes: Section 3.102.025B.6. A NO about the whole (S) document. Two separate scans of the extracted text found no 'fourteen', no '2031', no 'sunset' and no 'delete'. The only warrant references are 'unless required by law, warrant, or court order' for data sharing. Its only day counts are 30 days (policy changes, effective date) and 45 days (complaints). NEEDS SOFTENING. Write 'the text sets no fixed retention period' rather than 'allows unlimited retention', because the policy itself must set a limit.

claims.claim: The mayor's substitute defines surveillance technology as technology that conducts surveillance using fully or partially automated machine learning, artificial intelligence or similar technology.
claims.verbatim: primarily used, primarily designed, or primarily intended to conduct surveillance by using fully or partially-automated machine learning, artificial intelligence, or similar technology.
claims.notes: Section 3.102.005. Starts 'means any software, electronic device, system utilizing an electronic device, or similar technology'. It excludes technology used primarily for routine government functions, including building security, traffic management and civil code enforcement. The sponsors' (S-1) uses the same AI wording. This is the AI hook of the story, and it comes from the mayor's text, not the original.

claims.claim: The mayor's memo says the substitute focuses the definition on technologies that use artificial intelligence or other automated tools to locate and identify people.
claims.verbatim: This S-version focuses the definition on the new technologies people are most concerned about the ones that use artificial intelligence or other automated tools to locate and identify people.
claims.notes: On the page an em dash follows 'concerned about'; it is removed here to meet house style, so quote the two halves separately if printing. The preceding memo sentence says the old code definition 'was drafted to be broad, sweeping in ordinary items like digital cameras and smart phones.'

claims.claim: The mayor's substitute defines a license plate reader as a specialized camera and data system that captures and reads vehicle plates using optical character recognition.
claims.verbatim: means a form of surveillance technology that is a specialized camera and data system that automatically captures and processes images of vehicle license plates using optical character recognition.
claims.notes: Section 3.102.005. It continues 'ALPRs can identify plate numbers in real time or from recorded footage, and cross-reference them against databases to assist with law enforcement, traffic management, and security operations.' Compare with the original's broader wording in C16.

claims.claim: The mayor's substitute bars any contract that would materially expand a covered surveillance technology's capabilities without prior Assembly approval.
claims.verbatim: no contract may be executed that would materially expand that technology's capabilities without prior approval of the assembly in accordance with section 7.15.040G.
claims.notes: Section 3.102.006D.1, curly apostrophe normalized. The (S) text also states 'No municipal agency may sell surveillance data to any private person or entity' (3.102.006B.1).

claims.claim: The mayor's substitute exempts tests, pilots and evaluations of an expanded capability from that approval, so long as they aren't used for new surveillance of the public, and sets no time limit on them.
claims.verbatim: tests, pilots, evaluations, or other exploratory uses of an expanded capability
claims.notes: Section 3.102.006D.2. The 'no time limit' part is a NO about the (S) text, from the fetch model's reading; soften to 'sets no stated time limit'. Contrast with the original's 90-day cap and its explicit inclusion of free trials (C09, C10). The (S-1) carries the same exemption.

claims.claim: On September 15th the three sponsors laid on the table an S-1 version that they describe as targeted refinements to the mayor's S draft, keeping its overall structure and intent.
claims.verbatim: The proposed S-1 version makes targeted refinements to the S draft, sharpening privacy protections, clarifying definitions, and strengthening Assembly oversight without altering the overall structure or intent of the S version.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Assembly, AO 2026-108(S-1) and sponsors' memorandum
claims.notes: Read via r.jina.ai. The header reads 'LAID-ON-THE-TABLE' and '(S-1) Submitted by: Assembly Member McCormick Assembly Vice Chair Volland Assembly Member Scout'. Memo 'From: Assembly Members McCormick, Scout, and Vice Chair Volland', meeting date September 15th, AM number printed as 'AM XXX-2026'. The page shows 'S ‑1' with a non-breaking hyphen, normalized. The memo also calls its changes 'minor and primarily editorial'. Additions include Assembly approval before APD shares plate data with the Division of Motor Vehicles, and removing the qualifiers 'knowingly', 'materially' and 'consistently' from violation standards.

claims.claim: The sponsors' S-1 version strikes the original title's promises to limit the retention of surveillance data and to prohibit participation in external surveillance data networks.
claims.verbatim: TO LIMIT THE RETENTION OF SURVEILLANCE DATA
claims.notes: The fetch model reported both phrases, 'TO LIMIT THE RETENTION OF SURVEILLANCE DATA' and 'TO PROHIBIT PARTICIPATION IN EXTERNAL SURVEILLANCE DATA NETWORKS', as struck-through text in the S-1 title and memo subject line. Strike formatting is inferred from bracket markup in the extraction, so confidence is moderate. A full-text scan of S-1 found no 'fourteen', '2031', 'sunset' or 'delete'. NEEDS SOFTENING. Say 'the sponsors' September 15th S-1 text contains no 14-day deletion rule or 2031 sunset' only with 'as filed'. Don't say they abandoned it, because no source says which text they will move on October 20th.

claims.claim: APD's Safe Anchorage page states that APD doesn't use Flock cameras.
claims.verbatim: APD does not use Flock cameras.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Police Department, Safe Anchorage page
claims.notes: Read via r.jina.ai October 10th; the page is undated, so date_of_source is null. muni.org/safe and the muni.org SafeAnchorage.aspx page returned not-found or a blurb only; this anchoragepolice.com page is the live one. Alaska's News Source, October 5th, quotes the same sentence from APD's Real Time Crime Center page. 'does not' is APD's wording; write 'doesn't' in prose. date_of_source is the fetch date, the page is undated.

claims.claim: APD's Safe Anchorage page says all license plate data its readers scan is automatically deleted after 14 days.
claims.verbatim: All scanned data is automatically deleted after 14 days.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Police Department, Safe Anchorage page
claims.notes: Same page also says 'LPRs only log plate numbers and location coordinates' and 'All access is audited.' Traffic camera footage 'Every 3 to 5 days' is overwritten unless collected as evidence. This is APD policy as stated on its page, not code. Matches the 14 days in the original ordinance (C03). Undated page, fetched October 10th. date_of_source is the fetch date, the page is undated.

claims.claim: APD's Safe Anchorage page says the Anchorage Assembly banned municipal use of facial recognition technology in 2023.
claims.verbatim: municipal use of facial recognition technology was officially banned by the Anchorage Assembly in 2023.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Police Department, Safe Anchorage page
claims.notes: The page adds 'APD's technology does not use facial recognition.' The mayor's memo AM 603-2026 independently says chapter 3.102 'previously regulated the Municipality's use of drones, facial recognition, and body-worn cameras.' Note the original ordinance (C18) relocates rather than creates the facial recognition rule. Undated page. date_of_source is the fetch date, the page is undated.

claims.claim: Police Chief Sean Case said APD's license plate readers are enabled only in dashcams on patrol vehicles, according to Alaska's News Source.
claims.verbatim: license plate readers are only enabled in dashcams mounted on patrol vehicles
claims.notes: By Joe Allgood, published August 27th at 10:30 PM AKDT. Paraphrase of Case by the station, not a direct quote. Background. As of August 27th; may have changed.

claims.claim: As of late August, 238 cameras were registered with APD and 11 were integrated with its Real Time Crime Center, according to Alaska's News Source.
claims.verbatim: there are 238 cameras registered with APD
claims.notes: Also on the page: 'there are 11 cameras that have been integrated with APD'. Case quoted 'we know that the cameras exist, we don't have access to them' about registered cameras. Names Axon as a 'third party contractor'. APD's Safe page confirms the two tiers (registered Level 1, 'APD must obtain permission to access video'; integrated Level 2 through a CORE device) but gives no counts. Single-sourced counts, so attribute. Background.

claims.claim: The Assembly voted 8 to 4 to approve just under $600,000 to expand APD's Real Time Crime Center, according to Alaska Public Media.
claims.verbatim: The Assembly ultimately voted 8 to 4 to approve the crime center funding
claims.notes: By Wesley Early, published September 3rd. Amount phrase 'just under $600,000'. The Assembly's focus-on-public-safety page independently says the Assembly approved the RTCC audio-visual purchase, AM 524-2026, on September 1st. The vote count is single-sourced to APM. Background.

claims.claim: The expanded crime center system could reach up to 750 cameras across the city, according to Alaska Public Media.
claims.verbatim: up to 750 different cameras across the city
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. It's a capacity, not cameras installed; Chief Case said officers wouldn't access them all at once. Write 'could connect up to 750 cameras'. McCormick quote on the page: 'There's just so many red flags around this,'. Background.

claims.claim: In August, Chief Sean Case told the Assembly that Flock did not have a presence in Alaska at all, according to the Anchorage Daily News.
claims.verbatim: did not have a presence in Alaska at all
claims.notes: ADN's paraphrase frame with Case's quoted words; ADN adds it is no longer the case. No exact meeting date given by ADN (its link goes to an August 31st story). Alaska's News Source, October 5th, separately says Case told the Assembly on August 4th that APD's system is 'completely different' from Flock. Don't merge the two into one dated quote. NewsNation's August piece likewise says 'There are no Flock cameras in the entire state of Alaska'.

claims.claim: A newly installed camera at the South Anchorage Lowe's at 10900 Old Seward Highway was cut down late on October 4th, according to a report Lowe's filed with police.
claims.verbatim: at approximately 11:28 p.m. on Oct. 4, an individual cut down a newly installed camera
claims.notes: Re-verified from No.83 C66. Headline 'Flock camera cut down outside Anchorage Lowe's', by Jonson Kuhn and Courtney Simmons, published October 5th at 4:39 PM AKDT and since updated. Address 'located at 10900 Old Seward Highway.' Lead-in 'APD confirmed Lowe's filed a report stating that'. ADN, October 7th, independently reports APD confirmed 'an individual cut down a newly installed camera' late Sunday night at the South Anchorage Lowe's. The URL slug saying 'no report filed' is stale.

claims.claim: APD confirmed the downed device was a Flock camera and not a municipal streetlight, according to Alaska's News Source.
claims.verbatim: APD confirmed it was a Flock camera and not a municipal streetlight
claims.notes: Re-verified from No.83 C67. No APD primary statement fetched.

claims.claim: Flock said that the week before, it had begun installing license plate reader cameras for a private customer in Alaska.
claims.verbatim: Last week, Flock began installing license plate reader cameras for a private customer in Alaska.
claims.notes: Re-verified from No.83 C68. Statement from Flock media relations specialist Andrew Smith, quoted by Alaska's News Source and identically by ADN, October 7th. Not Flock's own page, so not primary. 'Last week' is relative to about October 5th. The station says Flock initially said on Monday it knew of no cameras in Alaska (paraphrase only today). Flock did not name the customer; do not name Lowe's as the customer.

claims.claim: Flock said its private customers can't access law enforcement data.
claims.verbatim: Private customers cannot access law enforcement data.
claims.notes: Flock statement via the station; ADN, October 7th, quotes the same line plus that private customers 'can only share their data directly, in a one-way relationship, with a law enforcement agency'. The verbatim keeps the source's 'cannot'; prose must say 'can't'. Attribute to Flock; it is the company's claim, not an audit.

claims.claim: Flock spokesperson Andrew Smith said every customer owns its data and controls who it is shared with, according to the Anchorage Daily News.
claims.verbatim: Every customer owns their data and controls who it is shared with.
claims.notes: Written statement to ADN. ADN says Flock did not say how the data is used, how long it is stored or whether it is shared.

claims.claim: APD spokesperson Regina Romero said the department has no access to license plate reader cameras installed at privately owned locations, according to the Anchorage Daily News.
claims.verbatim: does not have access to automatic license plate reading cameras installed at privately owned locations
claims.notes: Corroborated independently by Alaska's News Source, October 5th: APD 'does not have access to any video feed from that business.' KTOO, October 7th, also says Anchorage police told ADN it 'does not have access to the data from those cameras.'

claims.claim: The crowdsourced DeFlock map showed eight license plate reader cameras in the Municipality of Anchorage, four at the Midtown Lowe's and four at the Lowe's in Tikahtnu Commons, according to the Anchorage Daily News.
claims.verbatim: shows eight cameras within the Municipality of Anchorage
claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. A crowdsourced map, as reported by ADN, not an inventory; the Tikahtnu store is described as the east-side location. As of Tuesday, October 6th, DeFlock showed no operating cameras at the South Anchorage Lowe's (where one was cut down). DeFlock itself not fetched. KTOO says only that 'multiple Lowe's hardware stores in Anchorage installed some', citing ADN, so not independent. Write 'a crowdsourced map showed'.

claims.claim: Lowe's privacy statement says it keeps license plate reader data typically no more than 90 days and doesn't sell it, according to the Anchorage Daily News.
claims.verbatim: typically no more than 90 days (though shorter in certain states)
claims.notes: ADN quoting Lowe's privacy statement; Lowe's page itself was not fetched. Also quoted: 'We do not sell ALPR information and we only share it with select service providers' and the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children. Lowe's corporate communications didn't answer ADN's questions. Compare like with like. Lowe's 90 days is a private retailer's stated practice and APD's 14 days (C38) is police policy. The ordinance's 14 days would bind the city, not Lowe's.

claims.claim: The municipal clerk's office certified a recall petition against Mayor LaFrance on Monday, October 5th, according to the Anchorage Daily News.

claims.notes: NEEDS SOFTENING. This is the organizers' allegation, not a finding; ADN does not itself say the reports were late. ADN, September 16th, reports McCormick questioned vague and possibly missing information in the annual drone report and Municipal Manager Bill Falsey said the format had been accepted in the past and a revised report would come. Single-sourced; attribute.

claims.verbatim: That effort still needs to collect 7,225 signatures before a Dec. 7 deadline to go before voters on the April ballot.
claims.notes: Single-sourced; attribute. The April ballot is in a different calendar year (2027) if a year is printed.

claims.claim: Until recently Alaska was the only state without any Flock cameras, according to KTOO.
claims.verbatim: Until recently, Alaska was the only state without any Flock cameras.
claims.notes: Re-verified from No.83 C73. By Yvonne Krumrey. NEEDS SOFTENING; keep 'according to KTOO'. Consistent with NewsNation's August piece ('There are no Flock cameras in the entire state of Alaska', photo caption '49 states') and Case's August statement (C44). Next sentence: 'But multiple Lowe's hardware stores in Anchorage installed some, according to reporting by the Anchorage Daily News.'

claims.claim: The five cameras the DeFlock map showed in Juneau as of October 7th are all in city-owned parking garages and are made by Genetec, not Flock, according to KTOO.
claims.verbatim: The five cameras on the map as of Oct. 7 are all in Juneau's parking garages, owned and managed by the city.
claims.notes: Re-verified from No.83 C70 and C71 (curly apostrophe normalized). 'made by Genetec' per Deputy City Manager Robert Barr, used for parking enforcement, in place a few years, and otherwise only for missing persons cases with the city manager's office approval.

claims.claim: Juneau Deputy City Manager Robert Barr said "We don't have Flock cameras, and we don't have any plans to install them."
claims.verbatim: We don't have Flock cameras, and we don't have any plans to install them,
claims.notes: Re-verified from No.83 C72. Curly apostrophes normalized.

claims.claim: Assembly Member Keith McCormick told NewsNation "In Alaska, privacy isn't a privilege, it's a state constitutional right."
claims.verbatim: In Alaska, privacy isn't a privilege, it's a state constitutional right,
claims.notes: Headline 'Alaska is lone holdout with Flock cameras', by Steph Whiteside. The page shows only '1 month ago' and a photo caption dated August 3rd, so the article date is unconfirmed (date_of_source null); BACKGROUND, from before Flock reached Anchorage. Second McCormick quote on the page: 'The government should not maintain a searchable record where ordinary people go,'. ADN, October 7th, separately quotes McCormick that vandalism won't 'lead to lasting change'.

claims.claim: NOAA's Alaska Fisheries Science Center published a conversation with Acting Director Dr. Jamal Moss on its 2026 fisheries assessment process on October 7th.
claims.verbatim: 2026 Fisheries Assessment Process: A Conversation with Acting Alaska Fisheries Science Center Director Dr. Jamal Moss
claims.source_outlet: NOAA Fisheries, Alaska Fisheries Science Center
claims.notes: Page date October 07, 2026; credited to NOAA Fisheries' Office of Communications, no individual author. Story 2.

claims.claim: The Alaska Fisheries Science Center says it is addressing capacity challenges by pairing near-infrared spectroscopy with trained machine learning models to read otolith rings.
claims.verbatim: We're addressing capacity challenges by integrating advanced technologies such as Fourier Transform Near-Infrared (FT-NIR) Spectroscopy coupled with trained machine learning models to efficiently read otolith rings.
claims.source_outlet: NOAA Fisheries, Alaska Fisheries Science Center
claims.notes: Three returned segments joined. The page also says 'Increased sample throughput allows us to process more fish ages'. The page text never uses 'AI' or 'artificial intelligence'; say machine learning. Otoliths are fish earbones.

claims.claim: NOAA says Alaska produces more than half the seafood caught off the coast of the United States.
claims.verbatim: Alaska produces more than half the seafood caught in waters off the coast of the United States,
claims.source_outlet: NOAA Fisheries, Alaska Fisheries Science Center
claims.notes: Same sentence as C63.

claims.claim: NOAA puts the average wholesale value of Alaska's seafood at nearly $4.75 billion a year from 2020 through 2024.
claims.verbatim: with an average wholesale value of nearly $4.75 billion a year from 2020 through 2024.
claims.source_outlet: NOAA Fisheries, Alaska Fisheries Science Center
claims.notes: An average over five years, wholesale, not dockside. Keep 'nearly' and 'average'.

claims.claim: The center plans a cooperative research workshop in Spring 2027 with industry, fishers, scientists and coastal communities.
claims.verbatim: A first step toward this goal is a cooperative research workshop to be held in Spring 2027 that we are just beginning to plan.
claims.source_outlet: NOAA Fisheries, Alaska Fisheries Science Center
claims.notes: Future event, 'just beginning to plan'; write 'plans'. The workshop is to plan cooperative research projects for fiscal year 2028 (participant list per the fetch summary).

claims.claim: A 2023 NOAA study found the near-infrared and AI method estimates a fish's age in 30 to 50 seconds per otolith.
claims.verbatim: It takes just 30-50 seconds per otolith to estimate the age of the fish.
claims.notes: BACKGROUND (July 13th, 2023). Page prints an en dash in '30-50', normalized to a hyphen here. Same page says the method is 'more than 10 times faster than traditional methods'.

claims.claim: Researchers scanned 8,617 walleye pollock otoliths collected from 2014 to 2018 to train and test the models, according to NOAA.
claims.verbatim: 8,617 walleye pollock otoliths
claims.notes: Background. Verbatim is the fragment confirmed; the surrounding sentence was returned as a paraphrase.

claims.claim: NOAA scientists examine up to 40,000 otoliths from more than 15 species each year to determine fish ages.
claims.verbatim: Each year research scientists examine up to 40,000 fish otoliths of more than 15 species to determine their age.
claims.notes: Background, as of 2023. The October 7th page gives no annual figure.

claims.claim: About half of the audience polled at a Mat-Su Sentinel candidate forum favored prohibiting large AI and data center developments in areas such as Mat-Su, and most of the rest backed strict regulations.
claims.verbatim: About half favored prohibiting large artificial intelligence and data center developments in areas such as Mat-Su, while most of the remaining respondents supported strict regulations.
claims.notes: By Mat-Su Sentinel Staff, October 9th. NEEDS SOFTENING. An unscientific live audience poll ('Audience members used their phones to respond to live polling questions'); no response count or question wording given. The Sentinel ran the forum and reported its own poll. Write 'about half of those responding in a live audience poll'. Story 3.

claims.claim: The Sentinel forums hosted 22 candidates for Alaska House Districts 25 through 30 and Senate Districts M and O.
claims.verbatim: Alaska House Districts 25 through 30 and Senate Districts M and O
claims.notes: The count 22 came from the fetch summary; the district string is verbatim. Candidates introduced themselves and then listened; no candidate is quoted on data centers or AI.

claims.claim: About 200 residents attended the state-focused forum held Sunday, October 4th, at the Glenn Massey Theater in Palmer.
claims.verbatim: about 200 residents
claims.notes: Venue string 'held Sunday at the Glenn Massey Theater in Palmer'. The date October 4th comes from the photo captions. A second, borough-focused forum at the Palmer Depot on Thursday, October 8th, drew about 150 residents (paraphrase only). The article doesn't say which forum produced the data center poll.

claims.claim: A state proposal would move 30 square miles of rural land near Houston, Willow and Meadow Lakes from the Department of Natural Resources to AIDEA, with scalable data centers among the listed possible uses.
claims.verbatim: The proposed transfer would move 30 square miles of rural land from the Alaska Department of Natural Resources
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel, republished by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: BACKGROUND (August 18th, by Amy Bushatz). The proposal lists 'advanced manufacturing pads' and 'scalable data centers'. AIDEA says 'it does not mean any of it will be built' and no data center is approved. NEEDS SOFTENING. Say 'possible uses include'.

claims.claim: An ordinance to block data center construction within Houston city limits failed 4-2, according to the Mat-Su Sentinel.
claims.verbatim: An ordinance to block data center construction within Houston city limits failed 4-2,
claims.source_outlet: Mat-Su Sentinel, republished by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: Background. Callie Courtney and Lisa Johansen voted yes. The council separately approved two resolutions opposing DNR's transfer process unanimously. Council member Jeffry Brasel said 'There was zero transparency.'

claims.claim: The mayor's substitute AO 2026-108(S), as filed for September 15th, contains no fourteen-day deletion rule and no 2031 sunset for license plate readers.
claims.verbatim: contains a limitation, based on articulable operational needs, on the storage of surveillance data collected by ALPR that is not retained as evidence in a specific case or investigation;
claims.notes: This NO covers the whole AO 2026-108(S) PDF, ordinance plus the mayor's memo AM 603-2026, 14 pages, read via r.jina.ai. Three whole-text scans on October 10th found no 'fourteen', no '14 days' as a deadline, no '2031' and no 'sunset'. The verbatim is the storage rule (3.102.025B.6) used instead of a day count. Keep 'as filed' or 'the text read'. Don't say the mayor 'allows unlimited retention', because the policy itself must set a limit.

claims.claim: The sponsors' S-1 version laid on the table September 15th, AO 2026-108(S-1), contains no fourteen-day deletion rule and no 2031 sunset for license plate readers.
claims.verbatim: The proposed S-1 version makes targeted refinements to the S draft
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Assembly, AO 2026-108(S-1) ordinance text and sponsors' memorandum
claims.notes: This NO covers the whole AO 2026-108(S-1) PDF, 14 pages, read via r.jina.ai. Two whole-text scans on October 10th found no 'fourteen', no '14 days' as a deadline, no '2031' and no 'sunset'. Its deadlines are 30 days, 45 days and June 1. No source says which text the sponsors will move on October 20th, so don't write that they dropped the rule. Write 'the September 15th S-1 text contains'.

claims.claim: The sponsors' S-1 version uses the same definition of surveillance technology as the mayor's substitute, tied to machine learning, artificial intelligence or similar technology.
claims.verbatim: or similar technology primarily used, primarily designed, or primarily intended to conduct surveillance by using fully or partially-automated machine learning, artificial intelligence, or similar technology.
claims.notes: Section 3.102.005, re-fetched October 10th. Matches the (S) wording in C30 word for word. The old code definition appears in brackets as a proposed deletion.

claims.claim: The mayor's substitute requires the administration to send the Assembly its plate reader policy, and any material change to it, within 30 days.

claims.claim: The mayor's substitute would take effect 30 days after the Assembly passes it.

claims.notes: The verbatim is the mayor's memo. Code text 3.102.050(C)(1) and (C)(2), 'within 45 days of receiving a complaint about or internally detecting the violation, whichever is later'. 30 and 45 days are the only day counts found in (S).

claims.claim: The Assembly's ordinance page lists a second work session on AO 2026-108, its alternative versions and amendments for Wednesday, October 14th.

NOAA's Alaska Fisheries Science Center names machine-learning otolith ageing in its 2026 assessment process
Mat-Su forum audience splits on banning or strictly regulating AI data centers

killed.claim: The October 20th vote is on a 14-day deletion rule, a warrant rule and a 2031 sunset.
killed.why: Those numbers are in the August 18th original only. Both September 15th versions, the mayor's (S) and the sponsors' own (S-1), contain no 'fourteen', no '2031' and no 'sunset' in their extracted text. No source says which text is the October 20th vehicle. Use C03, C05 and C08 as 'the original version', plus C29 and C36.

killed.claim: The two versions going to a vote are the sponsors' AO 2026-108 and the mayor's AO 2026-108(S).
killed.why: The Assembly's own page lists three texts, the original, (S) and (S-1). (S-1) is the sponsors' September 15th refinement of the mayor's (S). ADN names no version numbers. Use C26 with its notes.

killed.claim: PDF AM 554-2026 is the ordinance text.
killed.why: It's the sponsors' two-page memorandum. The ordinance text is the separate AO 2026-108_1 PDF, which was read for C01 to C22. C04 is labeled as the memo.

killed.claim: AO 2026-108 would regulate private cameras such as the Lowe's Flock readers.
killed.why: The ordinance's core rules bind municipal agencies. Its private-camera provisions cover only registration and integration with the city (C19). Nothing in the original, (S) or (S-1) as read governs a private business's own plate readers.

killed.claim: The LaFrance administration's surveillance technology reports were late (as fact).
killed.why: It's only the recall organizers' allegation as quoted by ADN. ADN, September 16th, reports a dispute over the drone report's contents, not a finding that it was late. It survives only as C54, attributed.

killed.claim: Flock's private Alaska customer is Lowe's.
killed.why: Still unsupported. Flock didn't name the customer, ADN says Flock didn't share contract details and Lowe's didn't answer questions. ADN reports Flock readers mounted at Lowe's stores but never ties them to Flock's statement.

killed.claim: The South Anchorage Lowe's camera was Alaska's first Flock camera (as a flat fact).
killed.why: Still killed from No.83. No fetched page says 'first'. It survives only hedged, as C56 according to KTOO plus C47.

killed.claim: Juneau's license plate camera data is kept for a stated period.
killed.why: Still killed from No.83. KTOO gives no retention period, and Barr is unsure whether Genetec holds the data.

killed.claim: APD says no report was filed on the downed camera.
killed.why: Superseded. Only the URL slug says it. The current page says 'APD confirmed Lowe's filed a report'.

killed.claim: The original AO 2026-108 regulates artificial intelligence by name.
killed.why: A full-text scan of the original found no 'artificial intelligence' or 'machine learning'. The AI wording is in the mayor's (S) definition and memo (C30, C31) and carried into (S-1).

killed.claim: NOAA's October 7th message says the center uses AI to age fish.
killed.why: The October 7th page says 'machine learning' and never 'AI' or 'artificial intelligence'. Only the 2023 background page title uses 'AI' (C65).

killed.claim: Mat-Su candidates stated positions on AI data centers at the Sentinel forums.
killed.why: The Sentinel article quotes no candidate on data centers or AI. The figure is an audience poll (C68).
No fetched page says it. Alaska's News Source names only Axon, as a 'third party contractor' (see C41 notes).
